content.text: A failed Claude API call tells you who has to act. Most 4xx errors mean the request itself is wrong, and sending it again returns the same error. A 429, a 500 or a 529 is usually transient and worth retrying with backoff, which the official SDK already does twice by default. A loop that retries everything the same way hides bugs, ignores
and keeps hammering an API that has told you to stop.

On Monday morning, the ticket-tagging queue hasn't moved since Friday's switch to Claude Opus 5.5. No alert fired and the worker never crashed. Its log holds one line, repeated every second all weekend: a 400 saying "This model does not support assistant message prefill." The migration kept a prefilled assistant turn that newer models reject, and the worker's
retry loop turned a bug that should have failed on the first call into three days of silence.
"Any failed Claude API call should simply be retried in a loop until it succeeds." It sounds like resilience:

items.text: Networks drop connections and services have bad minutes, and "retry with
Some Claude API errors really are transient, and the docs themselves say to retry a 500 with exponential backoff.
In development, the only errors you meet are timeouts and rate limits, and a retry fixes both.
A loop that never gives up looks robust: nothing crashes and nobody gets paged.

content.text: The half-truth: retrying is the right answer for transient failures. But the status code already tells you whether a failure is transient, and a retry can't fix a request that's wrong.
The status code says who has to act
Every error comes back as JSON with an
. The docs list the codes, and sorted by who has to act, they fall into two groups:

rows.text: Fix the format or content of the request
Fix the API key or its workspace access
Send less: the Messages API accepts up to 128 MB
Unless it's the spend cap (see below)
Contact support with the request ID if it persists
The API is busy for everyone, not just you

content.text: join the "fix it" group. Two codes ask for a specific move instead of a blind retry: on a 409
the docs say to resolve the conflict, then retry, and on a 504
they point you to streaming for long requests. The docs also warn that the

The SDK already retries for you

From the errors page: "The official SDK automatically retries transient failures (such as connection errors, rate limits, and 5xx server errors) with exponential backoff, twice by default, honoring the
header when present." In Python, that covers connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and every status of 500 or above, and
on the client changes the count.

Wrap that call in your own loop of five and one bad minute becomes fifteen requests, most of them sent with a fixed one-second sleep that ignores how long the API asked you to wait. The non-retryable errors arrive at once, as typed exceptions:
. The docs' advice is to catch these typed classes "rather than string-matching error messages, handling the most specific classes first."
Not every 429 is a rate limit

are measured per model class in requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute, with a token bucket that refills continuously. Short bursts count: the docs' example is a 60 RPM limit enforced as 1 request per second. The 429 says which limit you hit, and its

header is "the number of seconds to wait until you can retry the request. Earlier retries will fail." A sharp jump in your traffic can also trigger 429s from acceleration limits, which is why the docs advise ramping up gradually.
Then there's the monthly spend cap of your usage tier. Reaching it also returns a 429

header, and usage pauses until 00:00 UTC on the first day of the next month. The docs are blunt: "Retrying, including the SDK's automatic retries, fails until access resumes." The body carries a code you can test:
A spend limit you set yourself, below the tier's cap, behaves differently again: it returns a 400
whose message starts with "You have reached your specified API usage limits".
A 429 is about your organization's limits. A 529

means "the API is temporarily overloaded", and the docs add that it "can occur when the API experiences high traffic across all users." Both deserve backoff, but your rate-limit headers won't explain a 529, and hammering an overloaded API makes it worse for everyone, you included. The first version treats every failure the same. The second lets the SDK handle short transient failures, decides what to do with each class that survives its retries, and lets request bugs fail on the first call:

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
tabs.code:
import time

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()


def tag(ticket: str):
    while True:  # "the API is flaky, retry until it works"
        try:
            return client.messages.create(
                model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
                messages=[
                    {"role": "user", "content": f"Tags for:\n{ticket}"},
                    {"role": "assistant", "content": "Tags:"},  # prefill
                ],
            )
        except Exception as err:  # a 400 loops here forever
            print(f"retrying in 1s: {err}")
            time.sleep(1)


tag("Customer reports a double charge on order 1042")

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import anthropic

SPEND_CAP = "enforced_spend_limit_reached"
client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # retries 408/409/429/5xx twice, with backoff


def tag(ticket: str):
    try:
        return client.messages.create(
            model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=1024,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"Tags for:\n{ticket}"}],
        )
    except anthropic.RateLimitError as err:  # still 429 after the SDK's retries
        error = err.response.json()["error"]
        if error.get("details", {}).get("error_code") == SPEND_CAP:
            raise SpendCapReached(error["message"]) from err  # page a human
        wait = int(err.response.headers.get("retry-after", 60))
        requeue(ticket, delay=wait)
    except anthropic.InternalServerError:  # 500 or 529 after the retries
        requeue(ticket, delay=300)
    # 400, 401, 403, 404 aren't caught: retrying can't fix them


tag("Customer reports a double charge on order 1042")

content.text: With the second version's handling, Friday's prefill bug would have raised

on the first call, with a message that names the problem. The docs suggest structured outputs or instructions in the system prompt in place of a prefill. A busy minute goes back to the queue with the delay the API asked for, and the spend cap reaches a person instead of a loop.

value the SDK would have honored. If you need full control, set

In a request a user is waiting on, keep retries short and fail fast. In a background worker, put the job back on the queue with a delay instead of sleeping inside the handler.

429, 500 and 529 are worth retrying with backoff, and the official SDK already retries them twice by default.

A 529 means the API is overloaded for everyone; a 429 means your organization hit a limit.
